Your car rolls uphill with the engine off at Magnetic Hill in Ladakh. It is a gravity-hill illusion, and the slope really runs downhill.
Your Google Maps shows all of Vatican City as a tiny dot you can walk across in minutes. It is a full country of about 0.44 square km.
Your map shows Lesotho, a whole country, sitting completely inside South Africa. The border circles it on every side.
Your trip from Poland to Lithuania can pass through a Russian region cut off from Russia. This is Kaliningrad, shown on the map.
Your walk in the French Pyrenees can end in Spain without leaving Spain. Llívia is a Spanish town surrounded by France.
Your car can drive on the Dead Sea shore, the lowest dry land on Earth. People float and read a newspaper on the water because of the salt.
Your sky and ground become one at Salar de Uyuni in Bolivia. After rain, the salt flat turns into a giant mirror.
Your eyes will not believe Lake Hillier in Australia. The lake is bubblegum pink from above.
Your night view of the Darvaza gas crater in Turkmenistan shows a pit of fire. It has burned since 1971.
Your photo of Danakil Depression in Ethiopia looks like another planet. Yellow, green and red acid pools sit on a hot salt desert.
Your idea of a tree breaks on Socotra, Yemen. Dragon blood trees are shaped like umbrellas and ooze red sap.
Your steps on the Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland land on about 40,000 interlocking, mostly hexagonal stone columns.
Your hike in Peru's Vinicunca shows a mountain striped red, yellow and turquoise. The colours are real minerals, and it is called Rainbow Mountain.
Your satellite view of the Sahara shows a giant bullseye. The Richat Structure is about 40 km wide.
Your beach at night in the Maldives can glow blue. Vaadhoo island waves light up with bioluminescent plankton.
Your Meghalaya walk crosses living root bridges. Villagers grew them from rubber fig tree roots over decades, and some are centuries old.
Your Maps view of Lonar in Maharashtra shows a round lake in a meteor crater. The lake water turned pink in 2020.
Your boat ride to Majuli in Assam lands on the world's largest river island, in the Brahmaputra.
Your satellite view of the sea between India and Sri Lanka shows a chain of shoals called Adam's Bridge or Ram Setu. It runs about 48 km.
Your drive in Bhutan's capital Thimphu has no traffic lights. A police officer directs the cars by hand.
Your flag drawing of Nepal needs no ruler. It is the only national flag that is not a rectangle, because it has two stacked triangles.
Your Everest summit photo is also a border photo. The Nepal-China border runs across the top.
Your Maldives holiday is on the lowest country on Earth. The highest natural point is only about 2.4 metres above sea level.
Your ferry ride in Istanbul crosses from Europe to Asia in minutes. One city sits on two continents.
Your phone clock in Russia has to handle 11 time zones in a single country.
Your flight from Paris can land in a French territory 12 or more time zones away. France has the most time zones of any country, because of its overseas lands.
Your whole town in Kiruna, Sweden is being moved. Buildings, and even a church, were relocated about 3 km because of mining.
Your climb on Ecuador's Chimborazo reaches the point farthest from Earth's centre. It beats Everest because of Earth's bulge.
Your evening at Wagah border near Amritsar shows India and Pakistan lowering their flags in a daily face-off ceremony.
Your step in Iceland's Thingvellir Park lets you walk between the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates, in a visible rift.
Your golf game in Haparanda-Tornio can cross two countries. The Sweden-Finland border runs through the course, with a one-hour time difference.
Your view of Lake Baikal shows ice so clear you see cracks and bubbles deep below. It holds about 20% of the world's unfrozen fresh water.
Your steps in Pamukkale, Turkey are on white terraces filled with warm blue water. Travertine formed them over time.
Your torch in Hang Son Doong, Vietnam lights a cave so big it has its own jungle and clouds.
Your ship in the Suez Canal seems to sail through sand. From the shore, huge vessels cross the Egyptian desert.
Your plane landing at Schiphol airport touches down about 3 metres below sea level. The Netherlands keeps the sea out with dikes.
Your border map of Liechtenstein shows a doubly landlocked country. You must cross two borders to reach any sea, as with Uzbekistan.
Your map of Chile shows a country about 4,300 km long and only about 177 km wide on average, a thin ribbon.
Your photo at Pangong Lake in Ladakh is taken on a lake that spans India and China. Its salt water freezes solid in winter.
Your rice field in Kuttanad, Kerala is below sea level. Farmers grow rice there behind bunds.
Your map of Oman and the UAE shows Madha, an Omani enclave inside the UAE, with a UAE village, Nahwa, inside it.
Your Jakarta trip is to a sinking city. Indonesia is moving its capital to Nusantara in Borneo partly because of that.
Your boat on Cambodia's Tonle Sap river sees the current flip. The river reverses direction every year with the monsoon.
Your satellite view of Dubai shows the Palm Jumeirah, an island shaped like a palm tree, built from sand in the sea.
Your Svalbard seed vault in Norway stores seeds from around the world inside a frozen mountain.
Your Amazon boat ride in Brazil reaches the Meeting of Waters near Manaus. Two rivers of different colours run side by side without mixing.
Your Venice trip has no cars. The whole historic city moves by boat and foot, with canals as the roads.
Your Sundarbans boat trip goes through the world's largest mangrove forest. It is shared by India and Bangladesh, and tigers swim between the islands.
Your Kutch visit in Gujarat lands on a white salt desert that looks like snow. The Rann turns into a shallow lake in the monsoon.
Your Angel Falls photo in Venezuela shows the world's tallest waterfall, with a drop of 979 metres. Much of the water turns to mist before it lands.
Your map of India shows the Siliguri Corridor, a strip of land only about 22 km wide at its narrowest that links the northeast states to the rest of India.
Your feet can stand in four US states at once at the Four Corners Monument, where Utah, Colorado, Arizona and New Mexico meet at a marker on the ground.
Your boat on Lake Constance floats where Germany, Austria and Switzerland never agreed on a border. There is no officially agreed line through the water.
Your photo of Lake Natron in Tanzania shows blood-red water. Its salty, alkaline water coats dead birds and animals in crusty mineral deposits.
Your dawn in Cappadocia, Turkey fills the sky with hundreds of hot-air balloons above rock chimneys, a sight famous around the world.
Your view of Zhangjiajie in China shows towering sandstone pillars wrapped in cloud. They inspired the floating mountains in the film Avatar.
Your camera in Antelope Canyon, Arizona catches a beam of light cutting down through smooth, wave-like orange rock carved by flash floods.
Your night hike at Kawah Ijen in Indonesia shows electric-blue flames pouring down a volcano. They are burning sulfur gas.
Your drive in Nevada passes Fly Geyser, a rainbow-coloured mound that spouts hot water. A drilling accident in 1964 created it.
Your river in Colombia, Caño Cristales, turns red, yellow, green and blue in the right season. It is called the river of five colours.
Your boat in the Waitomo caves in New Zealand glides under a ceiling of glowworms that looks like a starry night sky.
Your photo of Wave Rock in Western Australia shows a 14 m high granite cliff shaped like a frozen ocean wave.
Your walk across Monaco takes minutes. The whole country covers only about 2 square km and sits on the French Riviera.
Your rain gauge in Mawsynram, Meghalaya measures some of the heaviest rainfall on Earth. It is among the wettest places in the world.
Your trek into Deadvlei in Namibia shows black dead trees standing on white clay under red dunes, and they are roughly 900 years old.
Your commute in La Paz, Bolivia can be a cable car. The city's Mi Teleférico network is one of the largest urban cable car systems in the world.
Your road to Dhanushkodi, Tamil Nadu ends at a ghost town with sea on both sides, the Bay of Bengal and the Indian Ocean, wrecked by a 1964 cyclone.
Your boat on Loktak Lake in Manipur floats among phumdis, mats of vegetation. They carry the world's only floating national park, Keibul Lamjao.
Your boat on the Umngot river at Dawki, Meghalaya looks like it floats in the air because the water is so clear you see the riverbed.
Your letter can be posted from Hikkim in Himachal's Spiti Valley, home to one of the world's highest post offices at about 4,400 m.
Your calendar in Samoa lost a whole day. The country skipped 30 December 2011 when it moved across the International Date Line.
Your New Year in Kiribati arrives first. Its Line Islands run on UTC+14, the earliest time zone on Earth.
Your night sky over Lake Maracaibo in Venezuela flashes with lightning for hundreds of nights a year at the Catatumbo river mouth.
Your torch in the Cave of the Crystals in Naica, Mexico lights giant white gypsum beams as long as a bus, in a cave that is dangerously hot.
Your Google Street View of the Faroe Islands has sheep wearing cameras. Locals made 'Sheep View 360' because the islands lacked coverage.
Your satellite view of Lençóis Maranhenses in Brazil shows blue freshwater lagoons filling the gaps between white sand dunes after the rains.
Your map of Australia shows the Dingo Fence, a line of fence about 5,600 km long built to keep wild dogs out of sheep country.
Your drone view of the Great Blue Hole off Belize shows a perfectly round dark sinkhole in the reef, about 300 m across.
Your winter trek in Ladakh can be a walk on the frozen Zanskar river. Locals call this the Chadar trek.
Your visit to Chand Baori in Rajasthan shows a stepwell with about 3,500 steps in perfect geometric patterns, going 13 storeys down.
Your sunset at Burj Khalifa in Dubai can be watched twice. Ride the elevator to the top and the sun sets again.
Your drive through the Lærdal Tunnel in Norway lasts around 20 minutes. At 24.5 km it is the longest road tunnel in the world, with blue-lit caverns.
Your drive through the Atal Tunnel in Himachal runs 9 km under the Rohtang Pass and is the longest highway tunnel in the world above 10,000 feet.
Your train over the Pamban Bridge near Rameswaram waits as the middle span rises vertically for ships. It was India's first vertical-lift sea bridge.
Your walk to Mont Saint-Michel in France ends on a tidal island that the sea cuts off from land at high tide.
Your tide table in the Bay of Fundy in Canada shows a difference of about 16 m between low and high tide, the biggest tides on Earth.
Your sunrise and sunset at Kanyakumari happen over the same sea spot, where the Arabian Sea, Bay of Bengal and Indian Ocean meet.
Your satellite view of the Aral Sea in Central Asia shows rusting ships stranded in a desert where a huge lake once lay.
Your hike at Hierve el Agua in Mexico shows a waterfall frozen in stone. Mineral-rich spring water built the cliff formations.
Your boat in the Marble Caves of Patagonia, Chile glides through swirling blue and white rock chambers carved by the lake.
Your map of Spain's Rio Tinto shows a river as red as rust, tinted by iron and the acidic water of old mines.
Your stay in Matera, Italy can be inside a cave home. The old town, the Sassi, is a city carved into rock, now a UNESCO site.
Your underground trip in Derinkuyu, Turkey goes down about 18 levels into a city built for thousands of people, with stables and wells.
Your hotel room in Coober Pedy, Australia can be underground. Locals dig homes into the hillside to escape the desert heat.
Your boat on Lake Titicaca in Peru and Bolivia reaches the Uros people's islands, which are floating islands woven from reeds.
Your selfie at Victoria Falls on the Zambia-Zimbabwe border can be at the Devil's Pool, a natural rock pool on the very edge of the drop.
Your photo at the Statue of Unity in Gujarat shows the world's tallest statue at 182 metres, taller than the Statue of Liberty.
Your payment on the Pacific island of Yap can be a giant stone disc. Rai stones, some taller than a person, were used as money.
Your walk outside Longyearbyen in Svalbard has a rule: leave town and you need a rifle for protection against polar bears.
Your letter in Srinagar can be posted from the floating post office on Dal Lake, a post office housed on a houseboat.

Your walk across the Spanish border in Ceuta or Melilla puts you in Europe while standing on Africa's coast. These two Spanish cities are the EU's only land borders with Africa, shown by a fenced line on the map.
Your drive into the German town of Büsingen leaves you in Germany while every side of the road is Switzerland. The map shows a German pocket completely surrounded by Swiss land.
Your beach towel at Maho Beach on Sint Maarten has jumbo jets landing a few dozen metres overhead. The airport runway starts right behind the sand.
Your boat trip in India's Andaman Sea passes Barren Island, the only confirmed active volcano in South Asia. You can see smoke over black rock in the middle of the sea.
Your train ride in Goa passes right in front of Dudhsagar Falls. The railway bridge crosses the front of a four-tier waterfall about 310 m tall.
Your map of Puducherry shows one Union Territory broken into four separate pieces, Puducherry, Karaikal, Mahe and Yanam, sitting in three different states.
Your drive into Chandigarh lands in the capital of two states, Punjab and Haryana. The city itself belongs to neither, because it is a Union Territory.
Your map of Mumbai hides seven separate islands. Land reclamation joined them over time into the single city on the coast.
Your watch in the Assam tea gardens may run an hour ahead of India's official time. It is called Bagan time, and it exists so workers can use the early daylight.
Your camel ride in the Hunder dunes in Ladakh's Nubra Valley is on double-humped camels at over 3,000 m. Sand dunes sit in front of snow peaks.
Your safari in Gir forest in Gujarat can show the Asiatic lion. It is the only place on Earth where wild Asiatic lions live.
Your photo of Hampi in Karnataka shows a landscape of giant boulders balanced across the land, with ancient temples among them.
Your hike on Yanar Dag in Azerbaijan shows a hillside where fire burns straight out of the ground. The flames have burned for decades because natural gas seeps out of the rock.
Your night satellite view of Egypt shows one glowing green-and-gold ribbon in a black desert. It is the Nile, where the vast majority of Egyptians live.
Your phone battery would struggle in Oymyakon, Siberia, the coldest permanently inhabited place on Earth. A temperature of -67.7 °C was recorded there in 1933.
Your ferry ride to Hashima Island in Japan reaches a concrete city abandoned in 1974. It is called Battleship Island because of its shape, and it sits empty in the sea.
Your photo of Meteora in Greece shows monasteries built on top of tall sandstone pillars. Some are still reached by steps carved into the rock.
Your clock says midnight in Tromsø, Norway, and the sun is still in the sky. The sun does not set there for roughly two months in summer.
Your hike in Antarctica's McMurdo Dry Valleys ends at Blood Falls, where blood-red water flows out of the Taylor Glacier. The colour comes from iron in salty water.
Your map of Australia shows a country wider than the Moon. Australia is about 4,000 km east to west, and the Moon is about 3,474 km across.
Your map of South Africa shows three capitals: Pretoria, Cape Town and Bloemfontein. Each one holds a different branch of government.
Your rocket launch watched from Baikonur in Kazakhstan flies from land that Russia leases. The cosmodrome is inside Kazakhstan, and Russia pays rent for it.
Your walk through Nicosia, Cyprus, crosses the world's last divided capital. A UN buffer zone runs through the city, and you can see the barriers on the streets.
Your tour at Panmunjom on the Korean border includes blue huts that straddle the line between North and South Korea. Inside the meeting room, you can stand on both sides.
Your first view of Petra in Jordan is a huge Treasury building carved straight into rose-red cliff. The whole city was cut out of rock.
Your photo of the Chocolate Hills in the Philippines shows over 1,200 grass-covered mounds. They turn brown in the dry season and look like chocolate drops.
Your Mauna Kea in Hawaii is taller than Everest if you measure from its base, which is on the seafloor. It is about 10,200 m from base to peak, and most of it is underwater.
Your photo of the Easter Island moai shows giant heads in the grass. Excavations found that many of them have full bodies buried underground.
Your flight over the Nazca desert in Peru shows giant drawings of a monkey, a hummingbird and a spider on the ground. The shapes are best seen from the air.
Your walk in Chefchaouen, Morocco goes through a whole town of blue-painted walls and stairs. The old town is known as the Blue Pearl.
Your climb of Kilimanjaro in Tanzania ends on snow and glaciers, even though the mountain is near the equator.
Your night view of Nyiragongo in the Congo shows a glowing lava lake inside the crater. It is one of the largest lava lakes on Earth.
Your tour of Lalibela in Ethiopia shows eleven churches carved downward out of solid rock. Each church sits in a pit, with its roof level with the ground.
Your drive down the Avenue of the Baobabs in Madagascar passes giant baobab trees standing alone in a line. They tower over the road.
Your map of Afghanistan shows the Wakhan Corridor, a thin arm of land about 350 km long that stretches east until it touches China.
Your car on the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge has to switch sides of the road. Hong Kong and Macau drive on the left, and mainland China drives on the right.
Your road in Sweden used to run on the left. On 3 September 1967 the whole country switched to the right in one night, known as Dagen H.
Your map of the Pan-American Highway shows a road from Alaska to Argentina with a gap. The Darién Gap in Panama and Colombia has no road, about 100 km of jungle and swamp.
Your GPS at the Mitad del Mundo monument near Quito shows that the real equator is a few hundred metres away from the monument that carries its name.
Your GPS at the Greenwich Observatory places the zero line about 100 m from the famous brass Prime Meridian line, because the modern reference meridian sits to the east.
Your drive on the King Fahd Causeway crosses the sea from Saudi Arabia to Bahrain on a road about 25 km long.
Your drive over the Øresund Bridge between Denmark and Sweden drops into an undersea tunnel. The road goes underground at an artificial island called Peberholm.
Your photo at Jökulsárlón in Iceland shows glacier icebergs floating in a lagoon and washing up on a black sand beach, called the Diamond Beach.
Your map of Brasília shows a capital city built from nothing between 1956 and 1960. The plan looks like an airplane from above.
Your walk in Campione d'Italia leaves you in an Italian town that sits fully inside Switzerland, next to Lake Lugano.
Your hike up Mount Roraima in South America reaches a flat-topped mountain with sheer cliffs on every side, about 2,800 m high, where the clouds sit on top.
Your climb of Sigiriya Rock in Sri Lanka goes up about 200 m of sheer rock to the ruins of a fortress on top.
Your boat trip on Chilika Lake in Odisha crosses India's largest coastal lagoon, a brackish lake where you can spot Irrawaddy dolphins.
Your cruise through Ha Long Bay in Vietnam passes about 1,600 limestone islands rising from emerald water like green towers.
Your map of Bolivia shows two capitals: Sucre, the constitutional capital, and La Paz, where the government sits.
